en.title: Physical and Health Education: the whole course
en.short: This page covers what physical and health education is, how degrees are organised, main areas and study advice.

sections.heading: What the subject is
sections.text: Physical and Health Education (PHE) is the study and practice of human movement, physical activity, exercise, sport and health education. It asks how the body moves, how it responds to exercise, how movement skills are learned, how health knowledge and habits are formed, and how programmes can be organised safely and fairly. It prepares teachers, coaches, health promoters, sports administrators and researchers. Physical education and health education are connected but not identical. Physical education uses movement and games to develop the whole person. Health education builds the knowledge, attitudes and skills people need for health. PHE is not only sport, and it is not only classroom health talk.

sections.heading: How a degree is organised
sections.text:
Degrees and awards differ by country and institution, so check your own handbook and the current accreditation rules. In Nigeria, universities commonly offer a four-year bachelor’s degree, often a Bachelor of Education (B.Ed) or Bachelor of Science in Education (B.Sc.(Ed)), and colleges of education award the Nigeria Certificate in Education (NCE). Some polytechnics offer related National Diploma (ND) and Higher National Diploma (HND) awards. Master’s and doctoral programmes follow. In the United Kingdom, a bachelor’s degree commonly takes three years, and teacher training may be a separate postgraduate route. In Ghana, university bachelor’s degrees commonly take four years. These are general patterns, not promises about your school.

A programme usually combines general education, foundation courses in PHE, professional courses, teaching practice or field attachment, and a research project. The first year often introduces the field and basic science. Later years add teaching methods, adapted activity, management, assessment and research. Practical work, laboratory sessions and school or community placements are central. Ask your department which awards it is accredited to offer.

sections.heading: Main areas in teaching order
sections.text:
The introduction stage starts with the meaning, history and philosophy of PHE. It then builds the science base: anatomy and physiology for movement and health, foundations of exercise physiology, kinesiology and biomechanics, motor development and fundamental movement skills, health education foundations, and measurement with basic statistics.

The core stage applies this base. You study exercise physiology and training, applied biomechanics and movement analysis, motor learning and skill acquisition, sport and exercise psychology, and the sociology of sport and physical activity. Professional courses follow: curriculum development, methods of teaching physical education, adapted physical education and inclusion, sports administration and management, coaching and sports officiating, sports injuries, first aid and rehabilitation, health promotion and community health, school health and family life education, nutrition for health and exercise, assessment and evaluation, recreation, leisure and outdoor education, research methods, and professional ethics and practice.

At master’s level the work becomes more specialised and research-based: advanced exercise physiology and performance, sport pedagogy and curriculum theory, physical activity and public health, and research methods with a dissertation.

sections.heading: How to study it
sections.text:
Study the sciences with movement in mind. When you learn a muscle, name the action it produces. When you learn an energy system, link it to a running or ball game. Practise the skills you will teach, and watch others perform them. Keep a laboratory or field notebook with dates, measurements and what you observed.

Link theory to your own setting. Use local sports, school and community examples, but state clearly when a rule or health guideline belongs to one country. Health recommendations change, so check the current official source and give the date. Learn basic statistics early, because measurement, assessment and research depend on it. Form study groups, teach a topic to a classmate, and ask for feedback on your practical teaching.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text:
Many students treat PHE as only games or only health talk. The field needs both, plus science, teaching skill and administration. Others memorise definitions without being able to apply them in a lesson, a training session or a first aid case.

Safety is a common weak point. Do not copy an exercise programme without checking the person, the equipment and the setting. Do not present an outdated guideline as current. In research, do not confuse a correlation with a cause, and do not cite a source you have not read. Ignoring inclusion is another fault: adapted physical education is not an optional extra. Finally, check your own curriculum and accreditation rules instead of assuming that another country’s pattern applies to you.

keyPoints: PHE combines movement, sport, exercise science and health education; it is wider than games alone.
Degree length, title and accreditation vary by country and institution, so check your handbook.
Learn anatomy, physiology and biomechanics by linking them to real movements and skills.
Practical teaching, safety, inclusion and measurement are central, not optional.
Health guidelines and regulations change; use current official sources and name the country.
At master’s level, expect more specialised theory, critical reading and a supervised dissertation.

en.title: What Is Physical and Health Education?
en.short: Definitions, aims, scope, links to sport and recreation, careers and misconceptions in PHE.

sections.heading: Definitions and aims
sections.text: Physical education (PE) is a planned, sequential school programme that uses movement and physical activity to develop physical competence, knowledge, skills and attitudes for active living. Health education is planned learning that helps people understand health, build health literacy, the ability to use health information, and make informed decisions. PE aims at movement skills, fitness, teamwork and fair play; health education aims at knowledge, decision-making, communication and healthy habits. Both are educational, not merely sporting. Their scope is broad: PE covers games, dance, gymnastics, athletics, outdoor activity and fitness; health education covers personal health, nutrition, safety, disease prevention, mental health and family life. Content and names vary by country.

sections.heading: Relationship and limits
sections.text: The two fields overlap. PE gives learners practice in activity, safety and teamwork; health education gives the knowledge and reasoning that support safe, informed choices. Neither is the same as sport or recreation. Sport is organised, competitive activity with rules and performance aims. Recreation is voluntary leisure chosen for enjoyment or restoration. PE may include sport and recreation, but its purpose is education for all learners, including those who are less skilled or have disabilities. Health education is not only giving facts; it seeks skills and behaviour. A school lesson on warming up before a run, paired with a health education discussion of hydration, shows the link.

sections.heading: Careers and misconceptions
sections.text: Career paths include school PE teaching, coaching, community health work, public health, fitness instruction, recreation leadership and sports administration. Requirements differ by country and role; some need a degree, teaching licence or further training. Common misconceptions are that PE is only for talented athletes, that it is just games, and that health education is only first aid or moral instruction. In a community setting, a youth club in Accra might run a football session, then a short health education talk on hand washing and safe water. The football draws people in; the education aims at knowledge and action. Check local regulations and job requirements.

keyPoints: Physical education is a planned school programme that uses movement to develop competence, knowledge and attitudes for active living.
Health education is planned learning that builds health literacy and informed health decisions.
PE and health education overlap but have different aims: movement competence and health literacy.
Sport is organised competitive activity; recreation is voluntary leisure; PE may include both but is educational and inclusive.
Career paths include teaching, coaching, community health, fitness, recreation and sports administration, with requirements varying by country.
Common misconceptions are that PE is only for athletes or just games, and that health education is only facts or first aid.

en.title: History and Philosophy of Physical and Health Education
en.short: From ancient and African traditions to school systems, and the philosophies that shape physical education.

sections.heading: Ancient roots
sections.text: Physical education is old. Ancient Greek schools used the gymnasium for running, wrestling and throwing. Athens linked bodily training with music and letters; Sparta stressed military fitness. Ancient China and India also tied exercise, breathing and hygiene to health and discipline. In medieval Europe, training for knights included riding and combat. Health education has roots in ancient rules on cleanliness, water and food, but organised school health teaching grew with public health in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries.

sections.heading: Modern school systems
sections.text: In the nineteenth century, European gymnastics and drill systems entered schools, and physical training became a school subject. Later, games, sports and health instruction were added. International bodies and teacher training helped spread programmes, but each country set its own curriculum. Modern physical education aims at movement skills, fitness, teamwork and lifelong activity; health education aims at knowledge, attitudes and skills for healthy living.

sections.heading: African and Nigerian
sections.text: In many African societies, physical activity was part of work, defence, initiation and celebration. Wrestling, running, dancing and archery taught strength, endurance, courage and community values. In Nigeria, colonial schools often used drill and games. After independence, teacher-training colleges and universities helped develop physical and health education as a school subject. Practice still varies between states and schools, so check current national and state curriculum documents.

sections.heading: Philosophies in practice
sections.text: Idealism holds that mind and ideas are primary; in PE it stresses character, respect and moral example. Realism holds that the world exists independently of mind; it favours anatomy, measured fitness and safe technique. Pragmatism judges ideas by their results; it favours learning by doing, problem-solving and student interests. Existentialism holds that each person creates meaning through choice; it favours personal goals, responsibility and reflection. Teachers usually blend these views. Case: Mr Okafor in Enugu teaches traditional wrestling. He uses idealism for respect, realism for safe holds, pragmatism for balance drills, and existentialism for each learner’s goal.

keyPoints: Physical education has roots in ancient Greek gymnasia and in traditional African movement practices.
Modern school PE grew from nineteenth-century gymnastics and drill, then added games and health teaching.
Nigerian PE developed through colonial drill and later teacher training and university programmes.
Idealism stresses character and ideas; realism stresses facts and measurable performance.
Pragmatism stresses learning by doing; existentialism stresses personal choice and meaning.
Teachers often blend philosophies, and curricula vary by country and state.

en.title: Anatomy and Physiology for Movement and Health
en.short: How six body systems support movement and health, and how the body keeps a steady internal state.

sections.heading: Systems in brief
sections.text:
Anatomy is the study of body structure; physiology is the study of how structures work. Movement needs the skeletal, muscular and nervous systems, while health depends also on the respiratory, cardiovascular and endocrine systems.

The skeletal system gives shape, protects organs, stores minerals and forms joints, where bones meet. The muscular system produces force. Skeletal muscle is voluntary and attaches to bone by tendons; ligaments join bone to bone. Smooth and cardiac muscle are involuntary.

sections.heading: Control and support
sections.text:
The nervous system has the central nervous system (brain and spinal cord) and the peripheral nervous system. Motor nerves activate muscle fibres in motor units. Proprioceptors, such as muscle spindles, sense position and movement.

Anatomical terms describe position: anterior is front, posterior is back, superior is above, inferior is below, medial is toward the midline, lateral is away, proximal is nearer the trunk, distal is farther. Muscles often work in antagonistic pairs, one contracting while the other relaxes.

sections.heading: Transport and breathing
sections.text:
The respiratory system moves air through the nose, trachea and bronchi to the alveoli, tiny sacs where oxygen enters blood and carbon dioxide leaves. The diaphragm and intercostal muscles drive breathing.

The cardiovascular system is the heart, blood vessels and blood. It carries oxygen, nutrients and hormones, removes wastes and helps control temperature. Cardiac output is heart rate × stroke volume. The endocrine system uses hormones from glands, such as adrenaline from the adrenal glands and insulin from the pancreas, for slower, longer-lasting control.

sections.heading: Homeostasis in exercise
sections.text:
Homeostasis is the body’s ability to keep a stable internal environment, such as temperature and blood glucose, by negative feedback.

During exercise, heart rate, stroke volume and breathing rate rise, blood flow shifts to working muscles, and sweating cools the body. Adrenaline and cortisol rise, while insulin usually falls. For example, Amina climbs four flights of stairs. Her breathing deepens, her heart beats faster and she sweats; after rest, feedback returns her rates toward resting levels. Training improves these responses; values vary.

keyPoints: Anatomy studies structure and physiology studies function.
The skeletal, muscular and nervous systems produce and control movement.
The respiratory and cardiovascular systems supply oxygen and remove carbon dioxide.
The endocrine system uses hormones for slower control of body functions.
Homeostasis keeps internal conditions stable through negative feedback.
During exercise, heart rate, breathing and sweating increase, and cardiac output equals heart rate times stroke volume.

en.title: Foundations of Exercise Physiology
en.short: Muscle contraction, energy systems, acute exercise responses, training principles and key definitions.

sections.heading: Muscle contraction
sections.text: Skeletal muscle contracts when a motor neuron stimulates a motor unit, a neuron and the muscle fibres it controls. The action potential releases calcium inside the fibre. Calcium lets myosin heads bind actin, forming cross-bridges. The heads pull actin filaments toward the centre of the sarcomere, the basic contractile unit. ATP is needed both for the power stroke and to detach myosin and pump calcium back. Without ATP, muscle cannot relax normally. Contraction is graded by recruiting more motor units and by firing them faster.

sections.heading: Energy systems
sections.text: Cells rebuild ATP in three linked ways. The ATP-PC system uses creatine phosphate to rebuild ATP fast for a few seconds, as in a sprint start. Glycolysis breaks glucose or glycogen without oxygen, producing ATP quickly and lactate; it supports high-intensity work for one to two minutes. The oxidative system uses oxygen in mitochondria to break down carbohydrate and fat. It is slower but yields much more ATP, so it dominates longer, moderate work. The systems overlap; the mix depends on intensity and duration.

sections.heading: Acute responses
sections.text: During exercise, heart rate and stroke volume rise, so cardiac output (heart rate × stroke volume) increases. Blood flow shifts to working muscle, and ventilation and oxygen uptake rise. Systolic blood pressure usually rises. Example: at rest, 70 beats/min × 70 mL/beat = 4.9 L/min. During exercise, 140 × 100 mL = 14 L/min. These responses deliver oxygen and fuel and remove heat and waste.

sections.heading: Definitions and training
sections.text: Physical activity is any body movement that uses energy. Exercise is planned, structured and repeated activity done to improve or maintain fitness. Fitness is a set of attributes such as cardiorespiratory endurance, strength and flexibility. Training applies principles: overload, extra work above normal; progression, increasing gradually; specificity, training the target quality; reversibility, losing gains when training stops; and recovery, allowing adaptation. A student who jogs twice a week for health is exercising; a runner who adds a weekly hill session before a race is training.

keyPoints: Muscle contraction uses the sliding filament mechanism: calcium allows myosin to bind actin, and ATP powers and releases the cross-bridge.
The ATP-PC system is fastest and lasts seconds; glycolysis is fast but limited; the oxidative system is slower and yields the most ATP.
Cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume, and it rises during exercise along with ventilation and oxygen uptake.
Physical activity is any movement; exercise is planned and structured; fitness is a set of trainable attributes.
Training principles include overload, progression, specificity, reversibility and recovery.
Energy systems overlap, and the dominant system depends on exercise intensity and duration.

en.title: Kinesiology and Biomechanics: Basic Concepts
en.short: Anatomical position, planes and axes, levers, force, torque, centre of gravity and Newton’s laws in movement.

sections.heading: Position and planes
sections.text: Anatomical position is the reference pose: standing erect, face forward, arms by the sides, palms forward, feet flat and forward. The sagittal plane divides the body into left and right; flexion and extension occur here, around a transverse axis. The frontal plane divides front from back; abduction and adduction occur here, around an anteroposterior axis. The transverse plane divides upper from lower; rotation occurs here, around a vertical axis. A runner’s knee lift is mainly sagittal-plane movement.

sections.heading: Levers
sections.text: A lever is a rigid bar turning about a fulcrum. In the body, bones are levers, joints are fulcrums, muscles supply effort, and body weight or an object is the load. In a first-class lever the fulcrum lies between effort and load, as when the head nods. In a second-class lever the load lies between fulcrum and effort, as in a calf raise: toes are fulcrum, body weight is load, calf muscles are effort. In a third-class lever the effort lies between fulcrum and load. Most limb levers are third class; in a biceps curl the elbow is fulcrum, biceps is effort, and the hand with a weight is load. Third-class levers favour speed and range over force.

sections.heading: Force, torque and balance
sections.text: Force is a push or pull, measured in newtons (N). Torque is the turning effect of a force about an axis: torque = force × perpendicular distance from the axis, in newton metres (N·m). A 20 N force applied 0.5 m from a joint gives 20 × 0.5 = 10 N·m. The centre of gravity is the point where body weight acts; in a standing adult it lies roughly in the pelvis. A lower centre of gravity and a wider base improve stability. Newton’s first law: a body stays at rest or moves steadily unless a net force acts. Second law: force = mass × acceleration (F = ma). Third law: every action has an equal and opposite reaction. A sprinter pushes back on the blocks; the blocks push the runner forward.

keyPoints: Anatomical position is the standard reference for describing movement.
The sagittal, frontal and transverse planes contain flexion-extension, abduction-adduction and rotation respectively.
A lever has a fulcrum, effort and load; most limb levers are third class.
Torque = force × perpendicular distance from the axis, measured in N·m.
Centre of gravity is where weight acts; a wider base and lower centre improve stability.
Newton’s laws are inertia, F = ma, and action-reaction.

en.title: Motor Development and Fundamental Movement Skills
en.short: Stages of motor development, fundamental movement skills, perceptual-motor development and suitable activities.

sections.heading: Stages of development
sections.text: Motor development is the change in movement ability across the lifespan. Broad phases are reflexive, rudimentary, fundamental and specialised. Reflexes dominate early infancy; rudimentary skills include sitting, crawling and standing. Fundamental movement skills appear in childhood, and specialised skills are refined for sport, dance or work. Ages vary between children and countries, so treat age ranges as guides, not rules. Development tends head to toe and centre outward, but individual differences are normal.

sections.heading: Fundamental skills
sections.text: Fundamental movement skills are building blocks for later activity. They include locomotor skills (running, jumping, hopping, skipping), stability skills (balancing, landing) and manipulative skills (throwing, catching, kicking, striking). Running has alternating support and a flight phase. Jumping has takeoff, flight and landing. Throwing needs force and accurate release; catching needs tracking and hand closure. Teach them playfully in varied settings. For example, a child throws a beanbag at a wall target, then catches a soft ball, then uses it in a small game.

sections.heading: Perceptual-motor development
sections.text: Perceptual-motor development is the growing link between the senses and movement. It includes body awareness, spatial awareness, directional awareness, temporal awareness, balance and coordination. A catcher tracks the ball with the eyes, judges speed and distance, and moves the hands to meet it. A runner uses an auditory signal to start and adjusts pace to space. Activities that help include mirror games, obstacle courses, rhythm games, target throwing and balancing tasks. Give clear, simple cues and allow repetition.

sections.heading: Factors and activities
sections.text: Many factors affect development: maturation, growth, health and nutrition, activity opportunities, instruction, practice, motivation, environment, culture and disability. A supportive home, school and community matter. For example, a coach in Ibadan sets a circuit for children: hopping, beanbag throwing, catching a soft ball, then a small-sided game. For adolescents, use modified volleyball, athletics, dance and fitness circuits. Match demands to ability, avoid early specialisation, and let every learner take part safely.

keyPoints: Motor development moves through reflexive, rudimentary, fundamental and specialised phases, but ages vary.
Fundamental movement skills include locomotor, stability and manipulative skills.
Running, jumping, throwing and catching are building blocks for sport and daily activity.
Perceptual-motor development links senses with movement through body, spatial, directional and temporal awareness.
Maturation, health, opportunity, instruction, practice, motivation and environment all affect development.
Use playful, varied activities and match demands to each learner’s ability.

en.title: Foundations of Health Education: Health, Wellness and Behaviour
en.short: Health, illness, wellness, determinants, health literacy, promotion and behaviour-change models.

sections.heading: Health and illness
sections.text:
Health is more than the absence of disease. The World Health Organization (1948) defines health as complete physical, mental and social well-being. This is ideal and hard to measure. Disease is a diagnosed disorder. Illness is the person’s experience of feeling unwell.

Wellness is an active process of making choices towards well-being; it has several dimensions, including physical, mental and social. A person can have disease and still pursue wellness.

sections.heading: Determinants of health
sections.text:
Determinants of health are conditions and factors that influence health. Biological factors include age, sex, genes and nutrition. Social factors include family, education, culture, safety and discrimination. Economic factors include income, employment and housing. Environmental factors include water, air, sanitation and climate.

Take Amina, who lives in a city with poor drainage. Rain floods her street, contaminates the well and children fall ill. The infection is biological. Low income limits safe water, poor drainage is environmental, and crowded housing is social. Health education alone cannot fix this; it needs engineering and policy.

sections.heading: Health literacy and promotion
sections.text:
Health literacy is the ability to obtain, understand, judge and use health information to make decisions. It includes reading labels, understanding risk and navigating services. Health promotion enables people to increase control over and improve their health.

The Ottawa Charter (WHO, 1986) names five actions: healthy public policy, supportive environments, community action, personal skills and reorienting health services. Health education is planned learning that helps people make informed decisions. It is one tool in health promotion.

sections.heading: Behaviour-change models
sections.text:
Behaviour-change models guide health education. The Health Belief Model says action depends on perceived threat (susceptibility and severity), benefits and barriers, cues to action and self-efficacy. The Stages of Change model describes precontemplation, contemplation, preparation, action and maintenance; support differs by stage.

Social Cognitive Theory says learning occurs through observation and is shaped by personal, behavioural and environmental factors; self-efficacy is central. For Amina’s family, a worker might show the risk, provide soap to lower a barrier, and ask a community leader to demonstrate handwashing.

keyPoints: Health is more than absence of disease; WHO defines it as complete physical, mental and social well-being.
Disease is a diagnosed disorder, while illness is the person’s experience of feeling unwell.
Determinants of health include biological, social, economic and environmental factors, and they interact.
Health literacy is the ability to obtain, understand, judge and use health information.
Health promotion enables people to increase control over their health; health education is one tool within it.
Behaviour-change models such as the Health Belief Model, Stages of Change and Social Cognitive Theory guide health education.

en.title: Measurement and Basic Statistics in Physical and Health Education
en.short: Variables, scales, tests, descriptive statistics, reliability, validity and score interpretation.

sections.heading: Variables and scales
sections.text:
Variables are characteristics that differ. An independent variable is changed or chosen, such as a training programme. A dependent variable is measured, such as heart rate. Discrete variables are counted, such as sit-ups. Continuous variables are measured, such as height.

Scales of measurement: nominal names groups with no order (sex); ordinal orders but gaps are unequal (fitness rank); interval has equal gaps but no true zero (temperature in degrees Celsius); ratio has equal gaps and a true zero (heart rate).

sections.heading: Tests and scores
sections.text:
A test is a standard task that gives a score. Physical and health education uses fitness tests, skill tests and health measures. Standardise instructions, equipment, warm-up and timing, and record the unit.

Raw scores need context. Compare them with norms for the same age, sex and activity level, or with earlier scores. A percentile rank gives the percentage of a reference group scoring at or below that score. Use scores to guide teaching, not to label students.

sections.heading: Describing scores
sections.text:
Descriptive statistics summarise scores. Mean = sum of values ÷ number of values. Median = middle value when ordered. Mode = most frequent value. Range = highest − lowest. Standard deviation (SD) shows typical distance from the mean.

Example: six resting heart rates are 60, 64, 68, 68, 72 and 76 beats per minute. Mean = 408 ÷ 6 = 68. Median = (68+68) ÷ 2 = 68. Mode = 68. Range = 76 − 60 = 16. Sample SD = √[Σ(x − mean)² ÷ (n − 1)] = √(160 ÷ 5) = √32 ≈ 5.7 beats per minute.

sections.heading: Reliability and validity
sections.text:
Reliability is consistency: a reliable test gives similar results on repeat testing or between raters. Validity is whether a test measures what it claims. A test can be reliable but invalid, such as a scale that always reads 2 kg too high.

Interpret with care. Measurement error is always present. Use valid, reliable tests, follow the protocol, and report the unit and norm group.

keyPoints: An independent variable is changed; a dependent variable is measured.
Nominal, ordinal, interval and ratio scales differ in order and true zero.
Mean = sum of values ÷ n; median = middle ordered value; mode = most frequent value; range = highest − lowest.
Sample standard deviation s = √[Σ(x − mean)² ÷ (n − 1)].
A test must be standardised and interpreted against suitable norms, not by raw score alone.
Reliability is consistency; validity is measuring what the test claims.

en.title: Exercise Physiology and Training
en.short: Acute and chronic training adaptations, safe FITT programme design and exercise intensity.

sections.heading: Acute responses
sections.text: During one bout, aerobic exercise raises heart rate, stroke volume (blood pumped per beat), cardiac output (volume per minute) and blood flow to active muscle. Ventilation and oxygen uptake rise. Muscle uses more oxygen and glycogen, and body temperature rises. Resistance exercise increases local tension and motor unit recruitment, with a short rise in blood pressure. These responses are temporary and return towards rest afterwards.

sections.heading: Chronic adaptations
sections.text: Repeated aerobic training enlarges stroke volume and raises maximal cardiac output, lowers resting and submaximal heart rate, and raises capillary and mitochondrial density and oxidative enzymes. Ventilation becomes more efficient, though lung volumes change little. Resistance training mainly increases muscle fibre size, motor unit recruitment and strength, and can strengthen bone and tendon. It gives less cardiovascular change than aerobic work. Aerobic work mainly improves fatigue resistance.

sections.heading: Designing safe programmes
sections.text: Use the FITT principle: frequency, intensity, time and type. Match the type to the goal, such as aerobic work for endurance or resistance work for strength. Begin at a tolerable level, warm up, cool down and progress gradually. A common public-health target is 150 minutes of moderate aerobic activity a week plus two strength sessions, but check current national guidance. People with disease, pregnancy or symptoms should seek medical advice before hard training.

sections.heading: Estimating intensity
sections.text: Set intensity by heart rate, rating of perceived exertion (RPE, felt effort) or the talk test. Maximal heart rate is often estimated as 220 − age, an estimate only. Heart rate reserve (HRR) = maximal heart rate − resting heart rate. Target heart rate = resting heart rate + (desired fraction × HRR). Example: age 20, resting 60. Maximal = 220 − 20 = 200. HRR = 200 − 60 = 140. At 60%: 60 + (0.60 × 140) = 60 + 84 = 144 beats per minute. At 80%: 60 + (0.80 × 140) = 60 + 112 = 172 beats per minute. Check it with RPE and the talk test.

keyPoints: Acute exercise raises heart rate, cardiac output, ventilation and muscle oxygen use, then these return towards rest.
Chronic aerobic training lowers resting and submaximal heart rate and improves stroke volume, capillaries and mitochondria.
Resistance training mainly increases muscle size, motor unit recruitment and strength.
Use FITT (frequency, intensity, time, type), start at a tolerable level and progress gradually.
Maximal heart rate is often estimated as 220 − age, and HRR = maximal heart rate − resting heart rate.
Target heart rate = resting heart rate + (desired fraction × HRR); for age 20 and resting 60, 60% gives 144 beats per minute.

en.title: Applied Biomechanics and Movement Analysis
en.short: Qualitative and quantitative analysis of gait, jumping, throwing and lifting, with force, torque, levers and injury.

sections.heading: Qualitative and quantitative
sections.text:
Qualitative analysis is trained observation against a checklist, often from front, side and back, with slow-motion video. Quantitative analysis measures variables such as time, distance, velocity, force and joint angle, then compares them with a standard or with the same performer over time. Both start with the aim: speed, height, accuracy or safety.

Gait is walking or running. A stride is one full cycle; a step is one foot to the other; cadence is steps per minute. In jumping, takeoff velocity depends on impulse. In throwing, force passes through a kinetic chain, meaning linked body segments, from legs and trunk to arm. In lifting, a wide base and a close load reduce stress.

sections.heading: Force, torque and levers
sections.text:
Force is a push or pull, in newtons (N). A force-time curve plots force against time; its area is impulse, and impulse = average force × time. Torque is turning effect: torque = force × perpendicular distance from the axis, called the moment arm. Levers have a fulcrum, load and effort. Many joints act as third-class levers, with effort between fulcrum and load.

Worked example: a 200 N force acts 0.25 m from a joint. Torque = 200 × 0.25 = 50 N m. At 0.50 m the same force gives 200 × 0.50 = 100 N m, so doubling the moment arm doubles torque.

sections.heading: Observing and correcting
sections.text:
Observe the whole action, then key points: base of support, centre of mass, joint angles, timing and follow-through. Compare with a model, but allow individual differences. Give one cue at a time, demonstrate, then re-observe. Example: a lifter rounds the back. Cue “chest up, load close”, reduce the load, and check again.

Injury risk rises when force is large, repeated, sudden or poorly aligned. Tissue tolerance is the load a tissue can bear, and it varies. Analyse the mechanism, not only the site. Refer pain or suspected injury to a qualified health professional.

keyPoints: Qualitative analysis uses structured observation; quantitative analysis measures variables such as time, distance, velocity, force and angle.
Gait terms include stride, step and cadence; jumping depends on impulse, throwing on a kinetic chain, and lifting on keeping the load close.
Impulse = average force × time, and it equals the change in momentum.
Torque = force × perpendicular distance from the axis; a longer moment arm gives more torque.
Many joints act as third-class levers, with effort between fulcrum and load.
Observe from several angles, give one cue at a time, and analyse injury by mechanism and tissue tolerance.

en.title: Motor Learning and Skill Acquisition
en.short: Theories, stages, feedback, practice schedules, transfer and retention in motor skill learning.

sections.heading: Theories of learning
sections.text: Motor learning is a relatively permanent change in the ability to perform a skill through practice. Information-processing theories treat the learner as a system that perceives, decides and acts. Adams’ closed-loop theory stresses feedback and error correction. Schmidt’s schema theory says learners store general rules, or schemas, not every movement. Ecological and dynamic systems theories stress the task, environment and self-organisation. No theory explains all learning.

sections.heading: Stages and feedback
sections.text: Fitts and Posner describe three stages. In the cognitive stage the learner needs explanation and demonstration. In the associative stage movements become smoother and practice refines them. In the autonomous stage the skill is fast, consistent and needs little attention. Feedback is intrinsic, from the senses, or augmented, added by a coach. Knowledge of results (KR) tells the outcome; knowledge of performance (KP) describes the movement. Give KP briefly and not after every trial to avoid dependence.

sections.heading: Practice and transfer
sections.text: Practice schedules arrange repetitions and rest. Massed practice has little rest; distributed practice spreads it over time. Blocked practice repeats one skill; random practice mixes skills and usually improves retention and transfer. Constant practice uses one version; varied practice changes conditions. Part practice breaks a skill into parts; whole practice teaches it as a unit. Transfer is the effect of earlier learning on a new task; it can be positive, negative or zero. Retention is tested after a delay without feedback.

sections.heading: Designing sessions
sections.text: Begin with a clear goal and a short warm-up. Demonstrate the skill, then give one or two cues. Start with part practice if complex, then move to whole practice. Use blocked practice for a new skill and random or varied practice later. Give concise KP after selected trials, then reduce it. Include rest to limit fatigue. End with a retention or transfer task. Case: a coach teaching Amina a basketball free throw uses blocked sets, then random shots after a sprint, and checks success later.

keyPoints: Motor learning is a relatively permanent change in skill ability caused by practice.
Fitts and Posner’s stages are cognitive, associative and autonomous.
KR gives outcome information; KP gives movement information.
Random and varied practice usually improve retention and transfer more than blocked practice.
Transfer can be positive, negative or zero.
Design sessions with clear goals, demonstration, suitable practice, concise feedback, rest and a delayed test.

en.title: Sport and Exercise Psychology
en.short: Motivation, arousal, anxiety, confidence, attention, group dynamics, mental skills and ethics.

sections.heading: Motivation and arousal
sections.text: Motivation is the direction and intensity of effort: what a person chooses and how hard they try. Intrinsic motivation comes from interest; extrinsic motivation comes from rewards or pressure. Arousal is general physiological and psychological activation. The inverted-U idea says performance rises with arousal to an optimum, then falls. The optimum varies by person and task: a sprinter may need high arousal, a golfer putting calm. Complex, fine skills usually tolerate less arousal.

sections.heading: Anxiety and confidence
sections.text: Anxiety is an unpleasant emotion from perceived threat. Cognitive anxiety is worry; somatic anxiety is bodily signs such as a fast heart rate. State anxiety is felt now; trait anxiety is a general tendency. Confidence, or self-efficacy, is belief in one’s ability to succeed at a task. It can support effort and persistence, but unrealistic confidence may reduce preparation. Anxiety is not always harmful: performers differ in seeing it as helpful or damaging.

sections.heading: Attention and groups
sections.text: Attention is selective focus of awareness. It can be broad or narrow, internal or external. A footballer scanning for a pass uses broad external attention; a free-throw shooter may use narrow focus. Distractions pull attention away from the task, and fatigue makes focusing harder. Group dynamics covers roles, norms, communication, leadership and cohesion. Task cohesion is shared commitment to the team’s work; social cohesion is interpersonal liking. Cohesion often supports performance and satisfaction, but the link is not automatic. Social loafing is reduced effort when individual contribution is not visible.

sections.heading: Mental skills and ethics
sections.text: Goals direct effort. Specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, time-bound goals work better. Process goals control actions; performance goals target personal standards; outcome goals depend on others. Imagery rehearses movement or feelings using the senses. Self-talk uses short cue words. A nervous hurdler might set a process goal of driving out low for the first three strides, image the first hurdle, and use the cue 'smooth'. Ethical limits matter: only trained, licensed practitioners should assess or treat mental health problems. Obtain informed consent, protect confidentiality, avoid guaranteed results, and refer beyond competence. Check national practice rules.

keyPoints: Motivation is the direction and intensity of effort, and it can be intrinsic or extrinsic.
Arousal is general activation; the inverted-U optimum varies by person and task.
Anxiety has cognitive and somatic parts, while confidence is task-specific self-efficacy.
Attention can be broad or narrow and internal or external, and distraction pulls focus away from the task.
Group dynamics include roles, norms, cohesion and leadership; social loafing can reduce effort.
Goal setting, imagery and self-talk are mental skills, and ethical practice requires consent, confidentiality and referral.

en.title: Sociology of Sport and Physical Activity
en.short: Sport sociology: socialisation, gender, class, ethnicity, disability, politics, media, doping and fair play.

sections.heading: Sport as institution
sections.text:
Sociology studies how sport and physical activity shape, and are shaped by, society. A social institution is a stable pattern of rules, roles and organisations, such as the family, school, religion or sport.

Through socialisation, people learn the norms, values and skills of a group. A child who joins a school team learns teamwork, discipline and also who is expected to lead or support. Sport can build belonging, but it can also reproduce exclusion.

sections.heading: Social divides
sections.text:
Gender is the socially learned roles and expectations attached to being male or female; it differs from biological sex. Class is a person’s economic and social position. Ethnicity is shared cultural identity, not a fixed biological trait. Disability studies contrast the medical model, which focuses on impairment, with the social model, which focuses on barriers such as inaccessible facilities. These divisions overlap.

Suppose a town in Kenya schedules a girls’ netball league during market work. Participation falls because the timetable clashes with existing duties, not because girls dislike sport. Changing the schedule is a structural fix.

sections.heading: Politics and media
sections.text:
Politics and sport meet in funding, hosting, governance and protest. Governments use sport for nation building and diplomacy; athletes may use it to speak about injustice.

Media, meaning newspapers, broadcasters and social platforms, select and frame stories. Framing is the angle or emphasis given to an issue. Heavy coverage of men’s football can make women’s sport seem minor. Commercial pressure can also shape schedules and rules.

sections.heading: Doping and fair play
sections.text:
Doping is the use of prohibited substances or methods to gain an unfair advantage. The World Anti-Doping Agency, WADA, coordinates anti-doping rules that many sports bodies adopt. Fair play means respecting rules, opponents and officials, not only winning.

Inequality affects doping too: well-funded athletes may have more testing and medical support, while poorer athletes face different pressures. Sociology does not excuse cheating; it asks how systems create temptation and who bears the cost. A balanced view supports clean sport and fair access.

keyPoints: Sociology examines sport as a social institution that shapes and is shaped by society.
Socialisation teaches norms and values, and sport can include or exclude people.
Gender, class, ethnicity and disability are overlapping social divisions that affect access.
Politics and media influence funding, governance, framing and visibility in sport.
Doping violates fair play, and WADA coordinates anti-doping rules adopted by many sports bodies.
A sociological view supports clean sport and fair access without excusing cheating.

en.title: Curriculum Development in School Physical Education
en.short: Curriculum models, aims, content, sequencing, integration, evaluation and national contexts in school PE.

sections.heading: Models and aims
sections.text: A curriculum is the planned learning experiences a school offers. Common physical education (PE) models include multiactivity, which samples many sports; sport education, which uses seasons, teams and roles; Teaching Games for Understanding, which starts with a modified game and a tactical problem; and health-related fitness, which centres on active living. Each model favours different aims. Aims are broad purposes, such as movement competence, health, fair play and lifelong activity. Objectives are narrower and measurable. A national syllabus may state aims, but teachers choose units and lessons to meet them.

sections.heading: Content and sequence
sections.text: Content selection asks what knowledge, skills and values are worth teaching. Planners consider age and stage, safety, facilities, equipment, class size, inclusion, local games and the syllabus. Sequencing arranges content from simple to complex and across years, often in a spiral: passing is revisited with greater pressure and decision making. A unit runs for several lessons, each building on the last. For example, a Kano school with one shared field might teach invasion games in mixed groups, using small-sided games and peer roles, rather than many separate sports.

sections.heading: Context and evaluation
sections.text: Integration links PE with other subjects. Heart rate can connect with science, fair play with citizenship, and measuring distances with mathematics. Integration should be genuine, not forced. National syllabi shape decisions, but local context matters. England’s National Curriculum physical education sets statutory aims. Nigeria’s basic education curriculum includes Physical and Health Education. Kenya’s Competency-Based Curriculum organises learning around competencies, and South Africa’s Curriculum and Assessment Policy Statement includes physical education within Life Skills and Life Orientation. Teachers adapt frameworks to climate, space, culture and resources. Evaluation judges whether aims, content, teaching and assessment fit together. Formative evaluation uses observation, checklists and pupil feedback during a unit. Summative evaluation uses tests, projects or reports. Evaluation asks whether students can access the work, whether the sequence builds learning, and whether aims were met. It should lead to changes in content, time, equipment or teaching style.

keyPoints: Curriculum models such as multiactivity, sport education, Teaching Games for Understanding and health-related fitness favour different aims.
Aims are broad purposes, while objectives are narrower and measurable.
Content selection considers age, safety, facilities, inclusion, local games and the national syllabus.
Sequencing moves from simple to complex and revisits skills in a spiral across years.
Integration links PE with other subjects, but it should be genuine and not forced.
National syllabi set frameworks, but evaluation should check alignment, access and local fit.

en.title: Methods of Teaching Physical Education
en.short: Planning, demonstration, class organisation, safety, questioning and inclusive teaching in PE lessons.

sections.heading: Planning and explaining
sections.text:
A lesson plan is a written guide to objectives, equipment, space, timing, safety checks and how learning will be checked. Practical plans use three phases: introduction and warm-up, main activity, and cool-down or summary. Objectives describe what students will be able to do. A theory lesson also needs a plan, with seating, board or screen, and discussion.

An explanation gives the purpose and two or three key cues in short, clear language. A demonstration shows the skill. Stand where all can see, show at normal speed then slowly, and use full or part demonstration. A mirror demonstration faces the class; a shadow demonstration stands beside them. Explain briefly, demonstrate, then let students practise.

sections.heading: Organisation and safety
sections.text:
Class organisation is the arrangement of space, groups, equipment and transitions. Use lines, circles, grids or stations. Give instructions before students move, use a clear stop signal, and set the next task before changing equipment. In large classes, use small groups with a leader, stations, or peer practice. Mixed-ability classes need differentiation: the same objective with different equipment, space, rules, pace or support.

For example, Mr Adeyemi in Lagos has 64 students and four balls for a passing lesson. He sets four grids of 16, one ball per grid, and gives each pair a target number of passes. Confident pairs pass with one touch; less confident pairs use a larger, softer ball.

Safety is part of planning. Check the surface for stones and glass, remove jewellery, and know the school’s first-aid and emergency arrangements. Follow local school and national guidelines.

sections.heading: Questioning, assessment and inclusion
sections.text: Questioning checks understanding. Ask open questions, allow wait time, and ask several students. Assessment for learning means using what you see and hear during the lesson to adjust teaching, not just to grade. Give specific feedback, such as 'turn your hip more'. Inclusive teaching uses clear instructions, visual cues, peer support and flexible grouping so all students can take part. Plan for the range in every class.

keyPoints: A practical lesson plan states objectives, equipment, timing, safety checks and how learning will be checked.
Explain briefly with two or three cues, demonstrate clearly, then give students time to practise.
Class organisation covers space, groups, equipment and transitions; clear routines matter in large classes.
Safety checks include the surface, equipment, jewellery and emergency arrangements, following local guidelines.
Assessment for learning uses questioning, observation and feedback during the lesson to adjust teaching.
Inclusive teaching differentiates task, equipment, pace, grouping and support so mixed-ability classes can all take part.

en.title: Adapted Physical Education and Inclusion
en.short: Disability, equity, legal duties and practical adaptations in physical education.

sections.heading: Key ideas
sections.text: Adapted physical education (APE) changes tasks, equipment, space or instruction so learners with disabilities can take part safely and meaningfully. Disability is not only a medical condition. The social model sees disability as the result of barriers in society and the environment; the medical model focuses on impairment. Inclusion means the learner belongs, is valued and can participate, not merely that they are placed in the class. Equity means fair treatment: different support so learners have a fair chance, rather than treating everyone the same.

sections.heading: Legal and ethical reasons
sections.text: Ethical reasons include dignity, fairness, equal opportunity, health and belonging. Physical education teaches movement, teamwork and confidence, so exclusion can limit a learner’s life. Legal duties differ by country. In the United States, the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA) requires physical education for eligible children with disabilities. In the United Kingdom, the Equality Act 2010 requires reasonable adjustments. Nigeria’s Discrimination Against Persons with Disabilities (Prohibition) Act 2018 prohibits disability discrimination, including in education. Check current official guidance, because rules vary.

sections.heading: Practical modifications
sections.text: Change rules: allow extra time, extra bounces, no elimination, rotating roles and small-sided games. Change equipment: lighter or larger balls, bell balls for visual impairment, adapted bats, visual schedules and high-contrast markers. Change space: shorter distances, clear boundaries, ramps, quiet zones and safe areas. Change instruction: short steps, demonstration, verbal and visual cues, sign language, peer buddies, task analysis and extra response time. For intellectual disability, use repetition and predictable routines. For autistic learners, reduce noise and offer a calm space. For chronic health needs, plan pacing and emergency action.

sections.heading: Case example
sections.text: In a Lagos secondary school, a learner named Chidi uses a wheelchair. In a basketball unit, the teacher lowers the hoop, uses a lighter ball, allows two-handed passes and a buddy, and rotates all learners through referee roles. Chidi plays a small-sided game under the same scoring rules. The class discusses what fair participation means, and the teacher records what worked.

keyPoints: Adapted physical education changes tasks, equipment, space or instruction so learners with disabilities can participate safely and meaningfully.
Inclusion means belonging and participation, while equity means giving different support so learners have a fair chance.
Legal duties vary by country; examples include IDEA in the United States, the Equality Act 2010 in the United Kingdom and Nigeria’s 2018 disability law.
Modify rules, equipment, space and instruction to remove barriers, not to lower expectations unnecessarily.
For sensory, intellectual, autistic and chronic health needs, use cues, repetition, quiet spaces, pacing and emergency plans.
Plan with the learner, record what works and check current official guidance and school policy.

en.title: Sports Administration and Management
en.short: Covers planning, organising, staffing, leading, controlling, budgeting, events, governance and risk in sport.

sections.heading: Management functions
sections.text: Sports administration runs sport programmes and facilities. Management is often described through five functions: planning, organising, staffing, leading and controlling. Planning sets goals, schedules and success measures. Organising arranges roles, resources and facilities. Staffing recruits, trains and deploys coaches, officials and volunteers. Leading motivates people and resolves conflict. Controlling compares results with plans and corrects gaps. These functions overlap; a school sports coordinator may plan, lead and control the same event.

sections.heading: Budgets and facilities
sections.text: Budgeting estimates income and spending before commitments are made. Separate capital costs (lasting items such as a pitch or building) from recurrent costs (regular costs such as maintenance, transport and stipends). Monitor actual figures against the budget. Example: a school inter-house event expects entry fees 40,000 and stall fees 20,000, total 60,000. Expenses are officiating 15,000, first aid 10,000, equipment hire 20,000 and publicity 5,000, total 50,000. Surplus = 60,000 − 50,000 = 10,000 currency units. Facility management covers booking, cleaning, safety checks, maintenance and access.

sections.heading: Events and governance
sections.text: Event management begins with clear objectives, then plans venue, schedule, entries, officials, communication, results and review. Governance is the system of rules, roles and accountability. A community club should have a constitution, a committee, minutes, transparent accounts and codes of conduct. Sports policy states written positions on eligibility, safeguarding, inclusion and behaviour. Policies must follow national law and the rules of the relevant federation; check current official sources.

sections.heading: Risk and control
sections.text: Risk management identifies hazards, assesses likelihood and severity, applies controls, and reviews them. Common controls include safe grounds, qualified first aid, supervision ratios, consent forms, insurance and emergency plans. Controlling uses records, attendance, budgets, incident reports and participant feedback. A concrete case: a community football programme notices repeated late finishes. The coordinator reviews the schedule, changes kick-off times, confirms transport and checks the change over two weeks. This is the control cycle in practice.

keyPoints: Planning, organising, staffing, leading and controlling are the core management functions.
Separate capital costs from recurrent costs when budgeting.
Budget surplus = total income − total expenses; check the arithmetic.
Event management covers objectives, venue, schedule, officials, communication, results and review.
Governance sets rules, roles, accountability and transparent accounts.
Risk management identifies hazards, assesses likelihood and severity, controls them and reviews.

en.title: Coaching and Sports Officiating
en.short: Coaching cycle, athlete development, session planning, welfare, communication and officials’ duties.

sections.heading: The coaching process
sections.text: Coaching is a planned cycle: analyse needs, set goals, plan and deliver practice, monitor progress, then review and adjust. The coach teaches technique and tactics, builds independence and models respect. Long-term athlete development (LTAD) organises training and competition over years using growth, maturation, skill and motivation, not age alone. Models differ, but most stress a broad movement base, suitable competition, recovery and individual readiness. Check the governing body’s current guidance.

sections.heading: Session planning
sections.text: Session planning starts with one clear objective. A safe plan states group, space, equipment and time, and includes warm-up, main practice, cool-down and a contingency. Activities should be progressive and differentiated, meaning adapted to different abilities. For example, Coach Amina plans a 60-minute football session: 10 minutes warm-up, 15 minutes passing, 25 minutes small-sided game and 10 minutes cool-down. The total is 10 + 15 + 25 + 10 = 60 minutes. She checks ground, water and first aid first.

sections.heading: Welfare and communication
sections.text: Athlete welfare means protecting health, safety and dignity. Coaches follow safeguarding rules, obtain consent, supervise properly, manage workload and refer injuries or medical concerns to qualified staff. Communication should be clear, calm and age-appropriate. Give short instructions, demonstrate, ask questions and give specific feedback. Listen to athletes and never use humiliation. Keep personal information confidential. In many countries, coaches must report suspected abuse under national child-protection law and federation policy; confirm local requirements.

sections.heading: Officials and fair play
sections.text: Officials apply rules and protect fair play. In football, the referee enforces the Laws of the Game, keeps time and score, manages safety and discipline, and may play advantage; assistants help with offside and touchlines. In athletics, starters, timekeepers and judges apply World Athletics rules and competition regulations, including false-start procedures. In basketball, referees, scorer and timer apply FIBA rules. Duties include pre-event checks, accurate recording, clear signals and reports. Officials must be impartial, consistent and free from conflict of interest. Rules differ by sport, age group and country, so check the current official rulebook.

keyPoints: The coaching process is a cycle of analysis, goal setting, planning, delivery, monitoring and review.
Long-term athlete development uses growth, maturation, skill and motivation, not age alone.
A session plan needs a clear objective, safe organisation and warm-up, main practice and cool-down.
Coaches must protect welfare, obtain consent and report suspected abuse under local law and policy.
Clear, age-appropriate communication and specific feedback support learning.
Officials apply the rules impartially and protect safety and fair play; rules differ by sport and country.

en.title: Sports Injuries, First Aid and Rehabilitation
en.short: Prevention, recognition, first aid and rehabilitation of common sports injuries, with return-to-play caution.

sections.heading: Prevention and recognition
sections.text:
A sports injury is tissue damage during sport. Prevention includes warm-up, conditioning, technique, protective equipment, safe surfaces and rules. Fatigue and previous injury raise risk.

Recognition means noticing the mechanism, pain, swelling, bruising, deformity or loss of function. A sprain injures a ligament (bone to bone). A strain injures muscle or tendon. Severe cases need referral.

sections.heading: Immediate first aid
sections.text:
For a wound, apply direct pressure with a clean pad, then clean and cover it. Refer deep, dirty or gaping wounds. For sprains and strains, protect, rest, ice, compress and elevate. Put ice in a cloth, not on skin, for short periods. Some guidelines favour early gentle movement over prolonged rest.

For a suspected fracture, immobilise, do not straighten, cover open wounds and refer. Case: Ama, a footballer in Accra, rolls her ankle. She stops, uses ice through a cloth, compression and elevation, and is referred because she cannot bear weight.

sections.heading: Concussion and referral
sections.text:
Concussion is a brain injury from a blow or sudden movement. Signs include headache, dizziness, confusion, nausea, poor balance and memory problems. If suspected, remove the player immediately. Do not allow same-day return. Refer for medical assessment.

Refer fractures, dislocations, severe wounds, suspected concussion, or injury with numbness, deformity or inability to bear weight. Red flags after head injury include worsening headache, repeated vomiting, seizure, weakness or drowsiness.

sections.heading: Rehabilitation and return
sections.text:
Rehabilitation restores function through progressive loading. It is guided by pain and aims to regain range of motion, strength, proprioception (sense of joint position) and sport-specific skills. Too much too soon can cause re-injury.

Return to play requires medical clearance, pain-free full movement, strength near the other side and passed functional tests. After concussion, follow a stepwise, medically supervised return. Early return raises re-injury risk.

keyPoints: Prevention uses warm-up, conditioning, technique, equipment and safe rules.
A sprain injures a ligament; a strain injures muscle or tendon.
Control bleeding with direct pressure and refer serious wounds.
For soft tissue injury, protect, rest, ice, compress and elevate.
Suspect concussion: remove from play and do not allow same-day return.
Rehabilitation is progressive and return to play needs medical clearance.

en.title: Health Promotion and Community Health
en.short: Health promotion models, community diagnosis, programme planning, communication and evaluation.

sections.heading: Models of health promotion
sections.text: Health promotion helps people and communities improve and protect health. A model is a simplified explanation of how change happens. The health belief model links behaviour to perceived threat, benefits and barriers. The stages of change model runs from pre-contemplation to maintenance. The social ecological model places health in individual, family, community and policy levels. The Ottawa Charter (WHO, 1986) lists five actions: healthy public policy, supportive environments, community action, personal skills and reorienting health services.

sections.heading: Diagnosis and planning
sections.text: Community diagnosis is a systematic study of a defined community’s health problems, needs and resources. It uses records, surveys, interviews, focus groups and observation. Programme planning turns findings into action: state the problem, set SMART objectives (specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, time-bound), choose activities, budget, assign tasks and plan evaluation. For physical activity, a community might map safe walking routes. For nutrition, it might work with market vendors on affordable foods. For communicable disease prevention, it might plan handwashing points and vaccination reminders. Involve local leaders and residents.

sections.heading: Health communication
sections.text: Health communication is the planned use of messages and channels to inform, persuade and support behaviour. Segment the audience by age, language or occupation. Use trusted channels: radio, religious leaders, schools, markets, SMS and community meetings. Pretest messages for clear language and local meaning. Avoid fear-only messages; give a practical action. For example, a campaign may say “Wash hands with soap after using the toilet” and show where water and soap are available.

sections.heading: Evaluation
sections.text: Evaluation judges whether a programme worked. Process evaluation checks delivery: were sessions held, who came, was the budget followed? Impact evaluation checks short-term changes such as knowledge or behaviour. Outcome evaluation checks longer-term changes such as disease rates or fitness. Choose indicators before the programme starts. In an invented example, 400 adults are surveyed and 240 report low activity: 240 ÷ 400 × 100 = 60%. If the target is 50%, 200 people should report low activity, so 40 people need to become more active.

keyPoints: Health promotion models explain behaviour and its social context; no single model fits every community.
Community diagnosis identifies needs and resources before planning begins.
SMART objectives make programme plans measurable and time-bound.
Health communication should use trusted channels, local language and pretested messages.
Evaluation has process, impact and outcome levels, with indicators chosen in advance.
Percentage = part ÷ total × 100; check targets against the baseline.

en.title: School Health and Family Life Education
en.short: School health programme components, family life education, adolescent reproductive health and HIV prevention.

sections.heading: Programme components
sections.text: A school health programme is a planned set of activities that protect and promote students’ health. Its three core components are health services, a healthful school environment and health instruction. Many programmes also build school-community links as a fourth element. Health services include screening, first aid, immunisation referral and care for minor illness, usually delivered with local health authorities. A healthful school environment means safe water, sanitation, waste disposal, safe buildings, food safety and a culture free from bullying. Health instruction is planned teaching about health in the curriculum. School-community links connect the school with parents, health workers, local government and other partners so that messages and services agree.

sections.heading: Family life education
sections.text: Family life education teaches knowledge and skills for family relationships, human growth, sexuality, values, decision-making and respect. It is not only about sex. It should match the learner’s age and stage, use correct terms, and involve parents and the community where policy allows. Content and consent rules differ by country, so teachers follow the national curriculum and school policy.

sections.heading: Adolescent health and HIV
sections.text: Adolescent reproductive health covers puberty, menstruation, reproductive anatomy, fertility, consent, safer behaviour, and access to confidential advice. HIV prevention includes correct facts about transmission, prevention, testing and treatment, and challenging stigma. Condoms and other prevention methods are discussed only where age, curriculum and law permit. Where included, abstinence and delay should sit beside clear, respectful information and skills.

sections.heading: Age-appropriate planning
sections.text: Age-appropriate means the content, language and examples fit the learners’ development and local law. A concrete case: Mr Otieno, a teacher in Kisumu, Kenya, plans an HIV lesson. Younger students learn how HIV is and is not transmitted, and how to treat classmates kindly. Older students learn about testing and where to get confidential services. He invites a local clinic nurse through the school-community link and uses anonymous question cards. No student is asked to disclose personal health status.

keyPoints: School health programmes commonly combine health services, a healthful school environment and health instruction, with school-community links often added.
Health services include screening, first aid and referral, while a healthful environment covers water, sanitation, safety and bullying.
Family life education teaches relationships, growth, sexuality, values and decision-making, not only sex.
Adolescent reproductive health and HIV prevention must be accurate, respectful and matched to age and local law.
School-community links help parents, health workers and the school give consistent messages and services.
Teachers follow the national curriculum and school policy, because content and consent rules differ by country.

en.title: Nutrition for Health and Exercise
en.short: Macronutrients, micronutrients, hydration, energy balance, body composition and safe eating for exercise.

sections.heading: Macronutrients
sections.text: Macronutrients are nutrients needed in large amounts and supply energy: carbohydrate and protein give about 4 kcal per gram, fat 9 kcal per gram. Carbohydrate fuels high-intensity exercise and is stored as glycogen in muscle and liver. Protein supplies amino acids for repair and adaptation; most active people meet needs through regular meals, and high intakes are not automatically better. Fat provides energy, carries fat-soluble vitamins and supports cells. Fibre aids digestion. Balance matters more than any single food.

sections.heading: Micronutrients and fluid
sections.text: Micronutrients are vitamins and minerals needed in small amounts. They do not supply energy, but they support metabolism, oxygen transport, bone health and immunity. A varied diet usually meets needs; routine megadoses are not advised. Hydration means replacing water lost in sweat and urine. Needs vary with climate, sweat rate, clothing, duration and intensity. Drink to thirst and monitor urine colour; for long or hot sessions, electrolytes may help. Avoid overdrinking, which can cause dangerous low blood sodium.

sections.heading: Energy and body composition
sections.text: Energy balance is energy intake minus energy expenditure. A positive balance tends to increase body mass; a negative balance tends to reduce it. Body composition divides mass into fat mass and fat-free mass. For example, a 70 kg athlete with 20% body fat has 70 × 0.20 = 14 kg fat and 56 kg fat-free mass. BMI is a rough screening tool and can misclassify muscular people. Waist circumference adds useful information.

sections.heading: Exercise eating and safety
sections.text: Before exercise, eat a familiar meal rich in carbohydrate, with protein, low in fat and fibre, about 1 to 3 hours beforehand; timing varies. After exercise, combine carbohydrate and protein and replace fluids. Rapid weight loss by dehydration, laxatives, diuretics or starvation is unsafe and harms performance. Supplements are regulated differently by country; check the national regulator, such as NAFDAC in Nigeria. Beware quick fat-loss or guaranteed performance claims, and check anti-doping rules because some products contain banned substances.

keyPoints: Macronutrients supply energy: carbohydrate and protein about 4 kcal/g, fat about 9 kcal/g.
Micronutrients support metabolism and health but do not supply energy; a varied diet is usually enough.
Hydration needs vary with climate, sweat and exercise duration; avoid both underdrinking and overdrinking.
Energy balance = energy intake − energy expenditure; body composition divides mass into fat mass and fat-free mass.
Pre-exercise meals are usually carbohydrate-rich and low in fat and fibre; post-exercise eating combines carbohydrate and protein.
Dehydration, laxatives, diuretics and starvation for weight loss are unsafe; check supplement claims and anti-doping rules.

en.title: Assessment and Evaluation in Physical and Health Education
en.short: Formative and summative assessment, test design, authentic tasks, grading, feedback, fairness and data use.

sections.heading: Assessment purposes
sections.text: Assessment gathers evidence of learning; evaluation judges it against a purpose. Formative assessment happens during teaching and guides learning. Summative assessment happens at the end and records achievement. In physical and health education (PHE), both are useful: formative asks where the learner is now, summative asks what has been achieved.

sections.heading: Building tests
sections.text: Good tests start with learning outcomes and a table of specifications, which maps content and skills to items. Use clear instructions, suitable language and enough time. For practical skills, a checklist or rubric with described levels is more valid than one mark. Trial the test, then check item difficulty, the proportion correct, and discrimination, whether stronger students score higher. Validity means measuring what is claimed; reliability means consistent results. Fairness means all learners can show learning, with adapted equipment, extra time where policy allows, and familiar examples.

sections.heading: Authentic assessment
sections.text: Authentic assessment asks students to perform realistic tasks: teaching a small group, officiating a game, keeping a fitness log, planning a health campaign, or demonstrating a movement sequence. Rubrics make expectations public and reduce bias. Use several sources, such as teacher observation, peer assessment and self-assessment, and keep records. A practical case: a student plans and leads a 15-minute activity. The rubric scores planning, safety, instruction, participation and reflection. Feedback names one strength and one next step, not only a grade.

sections.heading: Grading and data
sections.text: Grading turns evidence into a symbol. Criterion-referenced grading compares performance with stated standards; norm-referenced grading compares students with each other. State weights and rules in advance and check local policy, because pass marks and grade boundaries vary by country and institution. Example: skills 50%, knowledge 30%, fitness 20%. Scores 7/10, 8/10 and 6/10 give (0.5×7)+(0.3×8)+(0.2×6)=3.5+2.4+1.2=7.1/10. Feedback should be specific, timely and actionable. Use assessment data to reteach weak topics, adjust tasks and monitor progress; do not use it only to rank students.

keyPoints: Formative assessment guides learning during teaching; summative assessment records achievement at the end.
Test construction starts from outcomes and a table of specifications, with clear instructions and suitable items.
Validity is measuring what is claimed; reliability is consistency; fairness gives every learner a reasonable chance to show learning.
Authentic PHE assessment uses realistic performance tasks and rubrics, supported by observation, peer and self-assessment.
Criterion-referenced grading compares work with standards; norm-referenced grading compares students with each other.
A weighted score is the sum of weight times score, for example (0.5×7)+(0.3×8)+(0.2×6)=7.1; check local grading policy because rules vary.

en.title: Recreation, Leisure and Outdoor Education
en.short: Recreation, leisure, play, outdoor education, risk management and inclusive programme design.

sections.heading: Defining the terms
sections.text: Leisure is the free time a person has after work, study, sleep and necessary duties. Recreation is activity chosen during leisure because it refreshes, satisfies or gives enjoyment; it may be physical, social, creative or intellectual. Play is voluntary activity, often with rules made up by players, that is done for its own sake and is central to children’s learning. The terms overlap: a game of football after class can be leisure, recreation and play at once.

sections.heading: Benefits and programmes
sections.text: Recreation benefits health through movement, and it builds social skills, confidence, rest and community ties. Schools use recess, clubs, intramural competitions (within the school) and outdoor days; communities use parks, sports centres, youth groups and festivals. Programmes should be varied so that different ages, interests and abilities can join. In an invented case, a community centre in Ibadan runs a Saturday games club. It offers football, table tennis, dancing and board games, so members who dislike competition can still take part.

sections.heading: Outdoor education and risk
sections.text: Outdoor education uses the natural or built environment for learning: camping, hiking, orienteering, gardening, environmental study and adventure activities. It can develop teamwork, resilience and care for nature. Risk management is the planned process of reducing harm. It includes risk assessment, qualified leaders, consent and medical forms, weather checks, suitable equipment, clear boundaries, emergency plans and review after incidents. Supervision ratios and first-aid requirements differ by country and activity, so check local rules and governing-body guidance.

sections.heading: Inclusive design
sections.text: Inclusive programme design removes barriers so that everyone can take part. Ask participants what helps, then adapt equipment, rules, timing, cost, transport and communication. Offer choices, use small groups, train leaders in inclusion, and provide accessible venues and toilets. Respect culture, religion, gender and disability; do not assume a person cannot join. Review participation data and complaints regularly, and change the programme. Inclusion is a continuing process, not a single rule.

keyPoints: Leisure is free time; recreation is chosen activity within it; play is voluntary activity done for its own sake.
Recreation can improve physical health, social skills, confidence and community ties.
Schools and communities should offer varied programmes for different ages, interests and abilities.
Outdoor education uses the environment for learning and needs planned risk management.
Risk management includes assessment, qualified leaders, consent, equipment, emergency plans and review.
Inclusive design removes barriers and adapts activities, and it is a continuing process.

en.title: Research Methods in Physical and Health Education
en.short: The research process, designs, sampling, data collection, basic analysis, ethics and proposals.

sections.heading: The research process
sections.text: Research is a planned, systematic search for answers. In physical and health education (PHE), the process moves from choosing a topic, to reviewing literature, to stating a problem and question, to designing the study, collecting and analysing data, and reporting.
