A problem statement names the gap: what is not yet known and why it matters. A literature review summarises studies and shows how yours adds to them. Keep the question narrow. Instead of “exercise and health”, ask whether a 10-minute daily activity break raises students’ step counts over four weeks.

sections.heading: Designs and sampling
sections.text: A research design is the plan for answering the question. Common designs include cross-sectional surveys, which measure once; longitudinal studies, which follow people over time; experimental and quasi-experimental designs, which compare groups; and qualitative designs such as interviews. Sampling is selecting participants. Probability sampling gives each person a known chance of selection; non-probability sampling does not. State inclusion criteria and sample size. Do not claim a sample represents everyone unless it was drawn properly.

sections.heading: Data and analysis
sections.text: Data collection uses questionnaires, tests, observation, interviews or records. Choose tools that are valid (measure what they claim) and reliable (give consistent results). Analysis starts with cleaning data and checking errors. Descriptive statistics summarise: the mean is the total divided by the number. For heart rates 70, 72, 74, 76 and 78 beats per minute, the total is 370, so the mean is 370 ÷ 5 = 74. Percentages show proportions: 18 of 60 participants is 18 ÷ 60 × 100 = 30%.

sections.heading: Ethics and proposal
sections.text: Research ethics protect participants and trust. Informed consent means giving clear information about purpose, procedures, risks, benefits, confidentiality and the right to withdraw, then obtaining voluntary agreement. Children and other vulnerable groups need special care; parent or guardian consent and child assent may be required. Seek ethics approval from the relevant committee. A proposal states the problem, review, question, design, sample, tools, analysis plan, timeline, budget and ethics. Follow your institution’s format.

keyPoints: A research question should be narrow, answerable and linked to a clear problem statement.
A literature review shows what is known and where your study adds new evidence.
The design, sampling method and data tools must fit the question.
The mean is the total divided by the number; percentage is part ÷ total × 100.
Informed consent must be voluntary, informed and recorded, with extra protection for vulnerable groups.
A proposal states the problem, review, question, design, sample, tools, analysis, timeline, budget and ethics.

en.title: Professional Ethics and Practice in Physical and Health Education
en.short: Codes, consent, confidentiality, safeguarding, boundaries, equity and ethical referral in PHE.

sections.heading: Codes and authority
sections.text: A professional code is a written set of standards and duties. Codes differ by country and role, so check the current code of your teaching council, coaching body or health regulator. Common principles are competence, honesty, respect, safety and accountability. Authority is the power a teacher, coach or health educator has over learners. Because learners depend on you, use authority to guide and protect, never to humiliate or exploit. A code guides decisions and grounds reports.

sections.heading: Consent and confidentiality
sections.text: Consent must be informed, voluntary and given by someone with capacity. Explain what will happen, why and any risk. For minors, seek parent or guardian consent and the young person’s assent. In an emergency, act to prevent serious harm and explain afterwards. Consent also covers touch in skills teaching, photographs and data. Confidentiality means sharing personal information only with those who need it. Tell learners its limits: you may share to protect someone from harm or meet a legal duty. Record only what is necessary.

sections.heading: Safeguarding, boundaries and equity
sections.text: Safeguarding is the duty to protect children and vulnerable adults from abuse, neglect and avoidable harm. It covers supervision, changing rooms, transport and online contact. Boundaries are limits that keep relationships focused on learning. Avoid private one-to-one contact behind closed doors, personal gifts and social media friendships with learners. Case: Coach Musa offers to drive 15-year-old Ada home alone at night. Even with good intentions, this crosses a boundary. He should follow the transport policy, inform a guardian and ask the safeguarding lead. Equity means giving each learner what they need to take part fairly, through reasonable adjustments, not treating everyone identically. Case: Teacher Ngozi sees unexplained bruises and a student’s fear of changing rooms. She does not promise secrecy; she records facts and refers to the school safeguarding officer. Referral means passing a concern to someone with the right training or legal role. Ask who may be harmed, what the code requires, and who to tell.

keyPoints: A professional code sets standards and duties; codes differ by country and role, so check the current one.
Use authority to guide and protect learners, never to humiliate or exploit them.
Consent must be informed and voluntary; for minors seek guardian consent and the learner’s assent.
Confidentiality has limits: share only on a need-to-know basis and to prevent serious harm or meet legal duties.
Safeguarding requires safe supervision, transport and online contact, and prompt referral of concerns.
Equity means reasonable adjustments for fair participation, not identical treatment.

en.title: Advanced Exercise Physiology and Performance
en.short: Energy metabolism, fatigue, cardiorespiratory limits, thermoregulation, adaptation and evidence appraisal.

sections.heading: Energy and oxygen
sections.text: Energy metabolism converts food into ATP, the cell’s energy currency. At high intensity, phosphocreatine and glycolysis supply ATP quickly; oxidative phosphorylation in mitochondria supplies more ATP slowly and needs oxygen. The Fick equation links oxygen uptake (VO2) to cardiac output (Q) and the arterial-venous oxygen difference: VO2 = Q × (CaO2 − CvO2). VO2max is the highest rate reached during maximal exercise to exhaustion; the highest value in a test without a plateau is often called VO2peak. It reflects oxygen delivery and muscle extraction, not one alone. A plateau in VO2 with rising work rate supports a maximal test, but criteria vary.

sections.heading: Fatigue and heat
sections.text: Fatigue is a fall in performance with many causes. Peripheral factors include glycogen depletion, metabolite accumulation, impaired calcium handling and reduced force per fibre. Central fatigue means the brain reduces motor drive. Lactate is not the sole cause. Thermoregulation balances heat production and loss. In exercise heat, evaporation from sweat is the main route, but humidity limits it. Dehydration and high core temperature raise cardiovascular strain and impair performance. Heat acclimation, gradual exposure over days, improves sweat and plasma volume responses.

sections.heading: Adaptation and example
sections.text: Training adaptation follows overload, specificity and recovery. Endurance training can raise plasma volume, stroke volume, capillary density and mitochondrial enzymes; strength training changes neural drive and muscle size. Gains are individual and plateau without progressive load. Worked example: a cyclist produces 200 W for 10 minutes. External work = 200 J/s × 600 s = 120,000 J = 120 kJ. If metabolic energy used is 500 kJ, mechanical efficiency = 120 ÷ 500 × 100 = 24%. The rest appears as heat. Efficiency varies with task.

sections.heading: Evidence to practice
sections.text: Appraise evidence by design, sample size, effect size, confidence intervals and applicability. Systematic reviews and randomised trials rank highly for causal questions, but small studies and surrogate outcomes can mislead. Check whether participants resemble your athlete or patient and whether the protocol is feasible. Apply findings cautiously: monitor response, avoid copying elite practice blindly, and respect health screening and rules. Evidence changes, so check guidelines.

keyPoints: ATP is the cell’s energy currency; phosphocreatine and glycolysis supply it quickly, while oxidative phosphorylation supplies it slowly and needs oxygen.
The Fick equation is VO2 = Q × (CaO2 − CvO2), linking oxygen uptake to cardiac output and arterial-venous oxygen difference.
Fatigue has peripheral and central causes; lactate is not the sole cause.
In heat, evaporation from sweat is the main heat-loss route, and humidity limits it.
Training adaptation follows overload, specificity and recovery, with large individual variation.
Appraise evidence by design, effect size, confidence intervals and applicability, and remember mechanical efficiency = external work ÷ metabolic energy used × 100.

en.title: Sport Pedagogy and Curriculum Theory
en.short: Four learning theories compared, with their effects on PE assessment, inclusion and teacher development.

sections.heading: Four perspectives
sections.text: Behaviourism treats learning as observable change from stimuli, practice and reinforcement; the teacher sets tasks, models and corrects. Constructivism holds that learners build understanding from prior experience; the teacher designs problems and guides reflection. Sociocultural theory, after Vygotsky, sees learning as social participation mediated by language, tools and temporary support (scaffolding) within the zone of proximal development, the gap between solo and supported performance. Critical pedagogy, after Freire, asks whose knowledge and interests the curriculum serves. These perspectives can combine in one lesson.

sections.heading: Assessment and curriculum
sections.text: Curriculum theory asks what knowledge is worthwhile and who decides. Behaviourist curricula favour sequenced objectives and measurable outcomes, so assessment uses checklists and criterion-referenced tests of technique, judged against set standards. Constructivist curricula favour authentic tasks and portfolios, assessing understanding and problem-solving. Sociocultural assessment values participation, peer feedback and performance in context. Critical assessment asks who benefits from the test and includes student voice. A volleyball unit might combine a skill checklist, a game-play portfolio and a group discussion of fair access to equipment.

sections.heading: Inclusion
sections.text: Inclusion means removing barriers so all students can take part. Behaviourism can support it through explicit steps, prompts and praise, but may narrow the curriculum if used alone. Constructivism offers multiple routes to understanding. Sociocultural theory highlights peers, language, cultural tools and scaffolding. Critical pedagogy names exclusion, for example when girls, disabled students or poor students lack space or equipment. Good practice combines high expectations, adapted tasks and a climate that does not treat difference as deficit.

sections.heading: Teacher development
sections.text: Teacher development follows from theory. Behaviourist models use observation schedules and feedback on discrete behaviours. Constructivist models use action research and reflective journals. Sociocultural models use lesson study (joint planning and observation), mentoring and communities of practice (shared practice groups). Critical models use collaborative inquiry into power, policy and practice. Strong programmes combine these: a teacher in Lagos might analyse video of a lesson, discuss it with peers, and ask which students were silent and why.

keyPoints: Behaviourism treats learning as observable change shaped by practice and reinforcement, and favours sequenced tasks and measurable outcomes.
Constructivism sees learners as building understanding from prior experience, so teaching uses inquiry, problem-solving and authentic tasks.
Sociocultural theory treats learning as social participation mediated by language, tools and scaffolding in the zone of proximal development.
Critical pedagogy asks whose knowledge and interests the curriculum serves and challenges exclusion.
Each theory shapes assessment differently: checklists, portfolios, contextual performance or student voice.
Teacher development can use observation, action research, lesson study or critical collaborative inquiry, and strong programmes combine them.

en.title: Physical Activity and Public Health
en.short: Surveillance, correlates, determinants, policy, built environment and community interventions for population activity.

sections.heading: Surveillance and terms
sections.text: Surveillance is repeated, systematic collection of population activity data by survey or device. The WHO Global Physical Activity Questionnaire (GPAQ) and International Physical Activity Questionnaire (IPAQ) are common self-report tools; accelerometers measure movement directly but cost more. Self-report overestimates activity, so compare countries cautiously. A correlate is a factor associated with activity, such as age. A determinant is a factor understood to shape it, such as transport policy. Association is not proof of cause.

sections.heading: Correlates and determinants
sections.text: Activity is shaped at individual, social, environmental and policy levels. Correlates include sex, age, income and safety. Determinants include urban form, transport systems and cultural norms. The built environment means human-made surroundings: streets, pavements, parks and buildings. Walkability depends on connectivity, density, mixed land use and safety. In high-income settings car-dependent suburbs can reduce walking; in low-income settings active travel may be common, but unsafe or polluted routes can limit it. Do not assume one setting’s pattern fits another.

sections.heading: Interventions and policy
sections.text: Interventions act on people or places. Community programmes include mass media campaigns, walking groups, workplace and school programmes. Policy and built-environment actions include pedestrian and cycle infrastructure, public transport, parks, traffic calming and land-use planning. Trials and natural experiments show that multi-component programmes and environmental change can raise activity, but effects are often modest and uneven. Evaluation should measure reach, uptake, maintenance and unintended effects. National guidance and funding rules differ, so check local policy.

sections.heading: Evidence and equity
sections.text: Equity means fair opportunity to be active, not equal outcomes. Barriers include cost, disability, gender norms, crime and lack of safe space. Programmes can widen gaps if they reach affluent or active groups. Low- and middle-income countries often have less surveillance data and intervention evidence; imported tools need adaptation. In an invented example, 1,100 of 2,000 adults meet the aerobic guideline: 1,100 ÷ 2,000 = 0.55, or 55%. If 600 of 1,000 women and 500 of 1,000 men meet it, the gap is 60% − 50% = 10 percentage points. Report gaps by income and disability.

keyPoints: Surveillance uses repeated population surveys or devices, and self-report overestimates activity.
Correlates are associations; determinants are factors understood to shape activity.
The built environment and policy can change activity, but effects are often modest.
Community programmes work best when combined with environmental and policy support.
Equity means fair opportunity, and programmes can widen gaps if they miss disadvantaged groups.
Prevalence = people meeting a guideline ÷ total population; report gaps by income, disability and place.

en.title: Research Methods and Dissertation in Physical and Health Education
en.short: Advanced design, sampling, measurement, analysis, ethics, data management and dissertation writing in PHE.

sections.heading: Design and sampling
sections.text:
A dissertation starts with a narrow, answerable and ethically acceptable question. The design is the plan for collecting and analysing evidence. Quantitative designs test hypotheses with numbers; qualitative designs explore meaning; mixed methods combine both. Choose the design that fits the question.

Sampling is selecting participants. Probability sampling, such as random or stratified sampling, gives every eligible person a known chance of selection and supports generalisation. Non-probability sampling, such as convenience or purposive sampling, is common in PHE but limits generalisation. Justify the sample size. Example: if 240 students are invited and 180 consent, the response rate is 180 ÷ 240 = 75%. If 12 later withdraw, retention is 168 ÷ 180 = 93.3%.

sections.heading: Measurement and analysis
sections.text:
Measurement turns concepts into data. Validity means an instrument measures what it claims; reliability means it gives consistent results. In PHE, questionnaires, accelerometers and fitness tests need standard protocols, calibration and pilot testing. Report the unit, the device and the procedure.

Quantitative analysis describes data and tests differences or associations. Qualitative analysis codes interviews or field notes into themes. Trustworthiness in qualitative work is judged by credibility, transferability, dependability and confirmability. Critical appraisal means judging a study’s design, sample, measurement, analysis and bias before trusting its conclusions.

sections.heading: Ethics and data
sections.text:
Most studies need approval from an institutional research ethics committee before data collection; rules differ by country and institution, so check the current requirements. Informed consent explains purpose, procedures, risks, benefits, confidentiality and the right to withdraw. Vulnerable groups need extra safeguards, sometimes assent from minors and consent from guardians.

Data management covers coding, anonymisation, secure storage, backup and access control. Data protection law varies by country. Keep a codebook and an audit trail so another researcher can follow your decisions.

sections.heading: Writing and presenting
sections.text:
Write the dissertation in a clear structure, commonly introduction, methods, results, discussion and conclusion. Make one argument, support claims with evidence, cite sources accurately and avoid plagiarism. Present findings in labelled tables and figures.

In the oral examination (viva) or conference talk, state the question, method, main finding and limitation. Explain what the study adds and what it cannot claim. Check your institution’s format and submission rules.

keyPoints: Match the design to the research question; quantitative, qualitative and mixed methods answer different questions.
Probability sampling supports generalisation, while non-probability sampling limits it, so justify the sample.
Report response rate as consenting participants ÷ invited × 100% and retention as remaining ÷ consenting × 100%.
Validity means measuring what is claimed; reliability means consistency; use standard protocols and pilot tests.
Qualitative trustworthiness rests on credibility, transferability, dependability and confirmability; critical appraisal judges bias.
Get ethics approval and informed consent before collection, protect data under your country’s law, and present findings with their limitations.
